items.title: Is Raphael Warnock running for president?
items.summary:
Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-GA) has kept the door open on a presidential bid. | Finn Gomez/Getty Images 

The 2026 midterm elections were less than three weeks ago — and the new Democratic congressional majorities chosen by voters are still more than a month from taking office — but if the 2028 Democratic presidential primary isn’t fully underway, then at the very least, potential candidates are already starting to jockey for position. 

Some of that maneuvering was on display earlier this month at the fittingly named “What’s Next” political conference in Denver. The conference drew Democratic operatives, strategists, and presidential hopefuls from around the country — and Vox’s America, Actually podcast, where host Astead Herndon asked attendees for their thoughts about Democratic Party’s future. 

Herndon also sat down with one possible 2028 candidate: Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-GA). His background is especially relevant after the midterms: He’s the senior pastor at the historic Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta at a time when more Democratic candidates are embracing religious appeals ; and he’s a student of the civil rights movement, the legacy of which could be seen in surging Black turnout across the South after the Supreme Court rolled back parts of the Voting Rights Act. 

Warnock has kept the door open on a presidential bid ; his colleague Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) is also frequently discussed as a potential candidate .

Herndon and Warnock discussed how Democrats can win in the South following election victories by Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom and others; why Warnock…
items.t: Is Raphael Warnock running for president?

items.title: The real reason Senate leaders keep becoming incredibly unpopular
items.summary:
Chuck Schumer (D-NY) looks on as Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) speaks during a news conference at the Capitol on February 2, 2023. | Drew Angerer/Getty Images 

Sen. Chuck Schumer has led the Senate Democratic caucus for 10 years, and he’s now facing the most serious challenge to his post that he’s ever encountered.

Just as Democrats are about to take their largest majority since the beginning of Barack Obama’s presidency, Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Schumer for the role of leading that new majority. Van Hollen has won the backing of several senators so far, as well as various outside progressive groups .

In one sense, the reasons Democrats might want to move on from Schumer are obvious. Schumer is 75 years old, and is not a particularly charismatic messenger or compelling speaker. His personal positions on issues like US support for Israel , and his longtime cultivation of Wall Street and corporate donors, put him out of step with the Democratic base. And polls regularly show that he is extremely unpopular .

At the same time, the job of Senate majority leader also isn’t really about winning a national popularity contest. It’s about leading the Senate — a challenging remit that involves a multitude of tasks, including but not limited to setting the legislative calendar, crafting legislative and big-picture policy strategy, dealing with outside interest groups, coordinating with the speaker of the House and president, and trying to hold the majority in the next election.

And there’s another underappreciated part of the job: volunteering to be the one…
items.t: The real reason Senate leaders keep becoming incredibly unpopular

items.title: Samaritans is changing to help its volunteers | Letter
items.summary:
With rota volunteers struggling, it’s not unreasonable to modernise working practices, a reader writes in response to reporting of branch closures

As a newer Samaritan, I’m bemused by the resistance to change in your article (‘Is anyone up for a fight?’ The battle for the soul of Samaritans, 10 November) and letters (16 November). Sams is a magnificent organisation that runs on love and dedication, and of course volunteers who have given so much will be upset at branch closures. But it also keeps going only through heroic daily efforts by a core of committed volunteers, doing tasks often unnecessarily duplicated in each branch, above and beyond the taking of calls – itself one of the hardest volunteer roles imaginable.

The rota volunteers at my large inner-city branch struggle every week to fill our overnight shifts, when demand and distress are highest. Illness and life responsibilities frequently close our two-people shifts and, with them, a fair chunk of our national capacity in the early hours. It’s not unreasonable to look again at working practices barely changed since the 1970s, even if that does mean slightly bigger centres and home working (only for those who want it), which offer more resilience for our callers.
Name and address supplied
items.t: Samaritans is changing to help its volunteers | Letter

items.title: America’s most visited national park right now is inside GTA VI
items.summary:
In Grand Theft Auto IV, players start in a fictional version of the Florida Keys and can visit places like the Everglades. | Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive 

There are plenty of reasons to be excited for the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, which came out today. There are the heists, the incredibly realistic depictions of Florida , the surprisingly deep romance , and, you know, the car theft. It’s been 13 years since the last installment of the incredibly popular game series — basically an eternity in 2026 terms.

But personally, I’m interested in the pelicans in flight at sunset and the green scales of an iguana in the street, as seen in the game’s second trailer . There are more than 170 animals in the game, like alligators, manatees, and frogs. There are also 62 species of birds, and players can pull out binoculars and record them all in a logbook. 

Now I’m not a video game writer. I write about biodiversity. So this stuff is basically catnip for me, and I’m not the only one. There are Reddit threads full of excited birdwatchers who are saying that crime sprees will come second to birding in the new game, or that they want to get one of the game’s protagonists, Lucia, some cute birding outfits. The top comment in the New York Times’s review of the game says, “my roommate gets to play the actual game. I get to find all 67 [sic] species of birds. Truly a game for everyone.”

While most of the game takes place in Vice City, which is developer Rockstar’s take on Miami, players start in a fictional version of the Florida Keys and can visit places like the Everglades and…

items.title: Teachers are reeling from an existential crisis. You’re probably feeling it too.
items.summary:
Braxton Wimbley was crying every day. Her fifth year of elementary school teaching at a public school in Indiana was, by far, her hardest. It was 2022, the first full academic year without Covid restrictions, and her fourth-graders’ social skills were “pretty much nonexistent,” she told Vox. “Because they had spent so much time at home doing whatever they want to do, [they] didn’t have structure and didn’t know when a teacher tells you no, that means no,” Wimbley, now 29, said.

Her students’ parents weren’t much help. Wimbley could see their exhaustion and empathized with the intensity of spending so much time with their kid during the pandemic. “I had parents blaming me for their child’s reading level, their child’s inability to do basic math, and I mean everything,” she said. One parent blamed her for the fact that her fourth-grader read at a kindergarten level. “I was like, ‘That’s not my fault.’”

Right before spring break, Wimbley wrestled with whether this career she had felt called to — growing up, she idolized Miss Honey from Matilda — was even right for her anymore. It was a painful thing to consider. And then a few days later, she was punched by a student. “After that, I was like, ‘Okay, I’m done. This is it,’” Wimbley said. Physically, she was unharmed. Her emotional state was another story.

Why I reported this 

A few years ago, one of my best friends left her job as a middle-school math teacher. For nearly a decade, she’d loved it — and, as her friend, I found her extremely suited to the job. After the pandemic, however, she decided to make a pivot into a…
items.t: Teachers are reeling from an existential crisis. You’re probably feeling it too.

items.title: Barns full of birds from America’s biggest foie gras company just burned down
items.summary:
As this photo from the Monticello Fire Department captured, a sprawling fire burned down several barns at Hudson Valley Foie Gras, America’s largest foie gras producer. | Monticello Fire Department 

Early Thursday morning in upstate New York, a fire broke out at Hudson Valley Foie Gras — the largest US producer of foie gras. French for “fatty liver,” foie gras is a delicacy product that’s made by force-feeding ducks in the final weeks of their lives. 

The fire destroyed multiple barns, and while hundreds of young ducks and geese survived, it’s still unknown how many died. Commercial duck farms tend to house thousands of animals — and sometimes over 10,000 animals — per barn.

“The fire took off so fast, there was no way to get inside to stop the spread,” Charlie Kalinowski, chief of the Smallwood/Mongaup Valley Fire Department, told Radio Catskill.

Approximately 200 first responders from 37 fire departments responded to the blaze, and no humans were injured. Hudson Valley Foie Gras didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment, though a vice president at the company told Radio Catskill that they suspect it started due to an electrical malfunction, which hasn’t been confirmed by local fire officials. 

Allie Granger of the nonprofit Animal Welfare Institute told Vox that the cause of barn fires usually goes unreported, but when they are reported, electrical malfunction tends to be among the most common causes at relatively large operations like Hudson Valley Foie Gras.

This incident is expected to hit the US foie gras supply hard, as Hudson Valley Foie Gras is one…
items.t: Barns full of birds from America’s biggest foie gras company just burned down

items.title: How Uruguay built a national care system from the ground up
items.summary:
Imagine a family with two working parents who can drop off their 2-year-old at a neighborhood childcare center for the workday for little to no fee. Their 4-year-old goes to a free public preschool nearby. Across town, the mother’s 82-year-old father, who can no longer bathe or dress himself, is visited by a personal assistant the government mostly pays for, 80 hours a month.

It’s not a daydream, it’s just a normal day for many families in Uruguay. 

And it is not just for lower-income households. A little more than a decade ago, Uruguay passed a law declaring that care for children, seniors, people with disabilities, and caregivers themselves is a right, and has been working to make good on that promise ever since. The resulting National Integrated Care System, known as SNIC (Sistema Nacional Integrado de Cuidados), has become a model around the world for treating care not as a privilege but as public infrastructure.

Across the country of about 3.4 million people, the system now provides early childhood care for some 78,000 children , subsidized home assistants for more than 6,000 people with severe disabilities, and day centers and emergency call services for older adults — through a network of community-run childcare centers, certified care workers, and a national agency that coordinates it all.

The undertaking has been huge, and the buildout is still in process. But the reasons for it echo across other high-income countries right now, including the United States, namely: falling birth rates, an aging population, and generations of women who are no longer willing or…
items.t: How Uruguay built a national care system from the ground up

The three men sat around a comically large and reflective roundtable to discuss issues like reforming the United Nations, increasing the world’s supply of petroleum, and reducing the risk of nuclear war, which they all thankfully agree would be a bad idea.

A major nuclear treaty between the US and Russia lapsed nine months ago , and China has been a sticking point to negotiating a new one. In fact, all three countries are — in one realm or another — major obstacles to each other’s geopolitical ambitions.

items.title: The astonishing toll of America’s food stamp cuts
items.summary:
A child helps load boxes at a California food bank in January 2026.  | Paul Bersebach/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images 

As we head into Thanksgiving, a holiday dedicated to abundance and sharing, millions of Americans are struggling to afford groceries. Children, in particular, are at risk, their parents forced to choose between listening to their baby cry because they’re hungry or watch them shiver because they can’t pay for heating as the weather turns cold.

Many of us have felt the costs of everyday life getting steeper, squeezing people at the gas pump and the grocery store. But some folks are facing not only inflation but the loss of government benefits: Federal assistance for food has been drying up since the Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed last year. According to the estimates from the left-leaning Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, about 5.5 million people have fallen off of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (or SNAP) between the law’s passage in July 2025 and July 2026 — a 13 percent decline in just one year. About 2 million of the people who lost benefits are children. At this point, SNAP participation has reached a 17-year low, the lowest it’s been since the Great Recession, and not because people don’t need it.

items.t: The astonishing toll of America’s food stamp cuts

items.summary:
By all measures, Rocky (1976) is the most successful sport film of all time. Half a century on from its release, the story of small-time boxer Rocky Balboa – who rises to square up against heavyweight champion Apollo Creed — continues to capture our imagination.

Directed by John G. Avildsen, the film won the prestigious Best Picture and Best Directing Oscars in 1977. And the broader franchise, consisting of five sequels and three Creed spin-offs, has generated more than US$1 billion at the global box office.

Rocky resonates because it is the ultimate underdog story. The hero is flawed, yet faithful to his dreams – working to overcome his self-doubt. His final victory is not a boxing title, but in proving his worth.

items.title: Elizabeth Holmes went from a startup darling to powerful seductress – these gendered portrayals profited investors

Despite the countless books, podcasts, TV miniseries and documentaries, people continue to be fascinated by the fall of Elizabeth Holmes and her health-tech startup Theranos. We are now being offered a new insight into the founder through the much-hyped documentary, You Can See Everything.

The initial drama of the documentary takes places 34 days before Holmes started her 11-year prison sentence for investor fraud in 2023. In our research, we examined how Holmes was presented across promotional materials, tweets, talks and interviews over the ten year period from her initial appearance on the public stage in 2013 to the same period in which the documentary begins.

Valued at around US$9 billion (£7 billion) at its peak in 2014, Theranos claimed to have built a device that could run hundreds of lab tests from just a few drops of blood. Holmes and co-founder Sunny Balwani hid that the device could not in fact do what they said, leading to its 2018 shutdown and their convictions for investor fraud (and, in Balwani’s case, defrauding patients as well).

For many, the fascination in Holmes’s story lies in the hubris and deception…

items.title: African glamour: the bold women who styled, wrote and read Drum magazine
items.summary:
Drum magazine was an African institution in the 1950s and 1960s. Launched in South Africa, it would go on to publish five regional pan-African editions across eight countries.

Much has been made of the male reporters of the magazine, but a new open source book considers how women used it to shape their worldviews and opportunities. We spoke with media scholar Wanjirũ G. Mbure about Out For Glamour In Africa.

What was Drum?

Initially known as The African Drum, Drum magazine started in South Africa in 1951, three years after apartheid was signed into law. The system of white minority rule would violently disenfranchise Black South Africans.

This was particularly evident in cities like Johannesburg, where large numbers of Black South Africans migrated from rural areas to work on mines. With little investment in housing and social services, they were forced to live on the outskirts of the city.

Magazines thrived in this period, looking to appeal to growing European and African urban consumers. Drum’s founder, South…

items.summary:
A surprising thing has happened at the UN climate conference, Cop31, as it gears up to its conclusion in Antalya, Turkey. Negotiators are discussing how to cool the planet.

You might think this should not be surprising, but how to respond to the latest climate science was not on the agenda when the meeting started. Now, the summit’s latest draft decision explicitly recognises a role for carbon dioxide removal (CDR) alongside deep emissions cuts. This is a significant shift, driven by pressure from some of the countries most vulnerable to climate change – the small island states – in response to two alarming scientific reports in the last month.

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.

items.title: An atlas of vanished places: how climate change is rewriting the books on our shelves
items.summary:
On August 26, 2026, a huge mass of rock and ice broke away at an altitude of around 5,200 metres in the Himalayas. Within minutes, it became an avalanche of debris and water that hurtled down towards the Nepal-Tibet border, with such force that the seismic signals were initially mistaken for an earthquake.

The region’s glaciers are visibly retreating, and thawing permafrost may well have contributed to destabilising these Himalayan slopes. Above all, the Nepal landslide illustrates something that will only become increasingly familiar: places that appear stable can change almost without warning.

While events like the Nepal landslide have an immediate, devastating impact on the people who live in these environments, they also leave their mark in a less obvious sphere: literature.

items.title: Bond has always reflected the masculinity of his time – Robert Pattinson’s 007 will need to embody a new era
items.summary:
James Bond has always reflected the cultural anxieties and zeitgeist of his era.

Sean Connery’s Bond embodied the confident western post-second-world-war masculinity of the early cold war. George Lazenby brought the character’s emotional vulnerability to light, reflecting the upheavals of the late 1960s. Roger Moore’s performance, meanwhile, added camp humour, theatricality and escapism in the 1970s.

In keeping with Ian Fleming’s more psychologically complex literary creation, Timothy Dalton brought a darker, more ruthless Bond to the screen. Stripping away much of the Moore era’s comedy and camp, his portrayal foregrounded emotional intensity and moral ambiguity. This reflected late-cold-war anxieties as geopolitical certainties unravelled and new threats emerged.

items.title: Burundi’s refugees are under pressure to return: why some choose silence when they do
items.summary:
Burundi has experienced repeated cycles of political violence and displacement, notably following the assassination of President Melchior Ndadayé in 1993. Further unrest followed during an election-related political crisis in 2015.

These cycles of unrest have resulted in thousands of deaths and forced hundreds of thousands of Burundians to flee their country. Over the past two decades, more than 1.1 million have sought refuge in other countries, primarily in neighbouring Tanzania. Others have fled to Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda and further.

There’s growing pressure from the Burundian state, as well as from neighbouring host countries, including Tanzania, Uganda and Kenya, to encourage repatriation. This reflects a broader regional shift in which the continued presence of Burundian refugees outside their country is becoming increasingly conditional.
